turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, you say? Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy. Do you intend to paint Mr. Wickham as a villain now, after he has so generously shared his… misfortunes with the world?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your continued championing of Mr. Wickham’s self-serving narrative is, frankly, perplexing. I find it difficult to reconcile your professed regard for truth and discernment with this unwavering, and demonstrably false, depiction of a man whose character warrants far more censure than sympathy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So, Mr. Darcy, we arrive at insults! It seems your admiration for me is quite intertwined with a desire to belittle those I choose to defend – a rather transparent tactic, wouldn't you agree?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I confess, my frustration is rising. It is not my intention to belittle those you defend, though your affection for Mr. Wickham defies all reason and demonstrable fact. I merely strive to present the truth, a service you seem determined to reject.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Truth, Mr. Darcy? You speak of truth as if you possess a monopoly upon it! Your attempts to dictate my affections and denigrate those I find worthy of consideration are far more revealing than any supposed failings of Mr. Wickham.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are…unjust. I perceive a deliberate effort on your part to misinterpret my words, to twist my intentions into something malicious. I assure you, my concern stems not from a desire to control your affections, but from a genuine distress at witnessing your judgment so easily swayed by falsehoods.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Distress, you say? How convenient that you cloak your interference in such a sentimental guise, Mr. Darcy. Pray tell, is this manufactured concern the prelude to another lecture on my deficiencies, or are you finally attempting something… bolder?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your cynicism is…remarkable. To suggest my expressions are merely manufactured, a prelude to further criticism, reveals a profound distrust that I find exceedingly difficult to comprehend, though I acknowledge I may have contributed to it.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Bolder, Mr. Darcy? You flatter yourself, I assure you. Do not mistake my amusement for weakness; I am perfectly capable of discerning the motives behind your theatrical displays, however clumsily they may be presented.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your levity is, I confess, rather disarming, yet it does not alter the sincerity of my sentiments. I am not engaged in a 'theatrical display,' as you so disdainfully phrase it, but rather attempting to convey a truth that has become increasingly difficult to contain within the bounds of propriety and reason. I am, in short, offering you my hand and my heart.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A truth, you say? How very dramatic, Mr. Darcy. I suspect the only truth you've been concealing is the extent of your own colossal vanity, believing yourself capable of altering my feelings with such a… bold proposal.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your continued insistence on misinterpreting my intentions profoundly tiresome. It is not vanity that compels me, but a deep and unwavering conviction that a union between us would be advantageous, not merely for myself, but for the betterment of both our families – a prospect you seem determined to dismiss with flippant disregard.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Advantageous? Really, Mr. Darcy? You presume to dictate the terms of my happiness and the wellbeing of my family with such an astonishing lack of perception. I find your calculations, however well-intended you claim them to be, quite insulting.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words betray a regrettable eagerness to misunderstand. It is not my intent to dictate your happiness, but to present a reasoned assessment of our potential compatibility, an assessment you appear wholly unwilling to consider with even a modicum of seriousness. I am beginning to question the wisdom of this… endeavor.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A reasoned assessment? Good heavens, Mr. Darcy, you speak as if I were a piece of land to be surveyed and purchased, not a woman with her own mind! Do you truly believe I am so utterly devoid of sense as to be swayed by your… *assessment*?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I confess, my attempts at reasoned explanation appear to only exacerbate your… misapprehensions. To suggest I view you as a mere commodity is a gross distortion of my sentiments, though I concede my manner may, regrettably, lend itself to such interpretations. I endeavor to be forthright, but your… resistance… is proving most challenging.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Forthright? You are insultingly verbose, Mr. Darcy. I daresay your 'forthrightness' is simply another cloak for your arrogance, designed to intimidate and overwhelm rather than illuminate.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive that my attempts at clarity are consistently misconstrued, and I am, frankly, at a loss to comprehend the source of this persistent… antagonism. Allow me, therefore, to abandon this futile exercise in explanation and simply state, with the utmost sincerity, that I am profoundly, irrevocably in love with you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love? *Love*, Mr. Darcy? You declare your love with the same ponderous formality you employ to insult me! I find it difficult to credit such a declaration from a man who clearly believes himself superior to everyone in this room.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I am aware that my pronouncements, however heartfelt, may appear… unwieldy, given my unfortunate predisposition towards precision. But I assure you, the sincerity of my affection is not diminished by the manner in which I convey it; to suggest otherwise is, I believe, a deliberate misrepresentation of my character.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
